accuracy.evidence: Matches the topic's three evidence statements: naming the body part for each sense (eyes see, ears hear, nose smells, mouth/tongue tastes, hands feel), describing with a sense word (loud, soft, smelly, bumpy, prickly, sour), and knowing some things are for looking, not tasting. Checked against Development Matters (use all their senses in hands-on exploration of natural materials) and the Head Start ELOF scientific inquiry indicators. The adult text adds the one nuance a simplification could hide: touch is sensed by skin all over the body and hands are only the part children use most. Safety claims (park mushrooms and berries, soap, pills can poison) follow NHS poisoning advice.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the real slips of two- and three-year-olds: confusing which organ does what (challenge 'eyes' for a barking dog, 'mouth' for smelling a flower, the match step rejecting 'Your ears can not see a rainbow'), believing you only find out by looking (feely bag prediction, challenge 'never' and 'look'), using a word from the wrong sense (drum 'fluffy', lemon 'shiny', each answered 'Shiny is a word for your eyes'), and mouthing non-food (soap, crayon, park mushroom, a sweet on the floor, licking the pine cone stops the step).

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanics only make sense for the senses: dragging a thing onto one of five body-part tiles, a feely bag that refuses a guess until Feel is pressed and then gives only a touch description, sense-word cards checked against the sense icon shown, a food plate versus look-only box with a reason for each item, and a pine cone that returns a different finding for each body part while the mouth tile triggers a stop. The distinctness gate passed against every flagship lab, including flagfeel and flagask.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child finds each idea by doing it: the bag cannot be solved by looking, only by the felt clue (soft and fluffy leads to the teddy, hard and cold to the rock), so touch is discovered as a way of knowing; the pine cone gives brown scales to eyes, a click to ears, a tree smell to the nose and prickly bumps to hands, showing that more senses tell you more. Each finished task names the idea (eyes see, ears hear...; only taste food a grown-up gives you).

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'How do you know a bell is ringing? With my eyes / With my ears' (sending the bell to eyes is rejected), 'Can your hands tell what is in the bag? No, I need my eyes / Yes' (the bag is solved three times with no picture), and 'A red mushroom in the park looks yummy. Can you taste it? Yes, it looks yummy / No, just look' (dropping it on the food plate gives 'Some can make you very ill. Just look').

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with rotated answer order and a streak count. Each wrong answer names the slip: 'Eyes see the dog. Ears hear the bark', 'Looking can not tell you soft. Gentle hands can', 'Do not lick it! Mouths are only for food from a grown-up', 'Never eat things from the floor. Tell a grown-up', 'Sweet is a taste word. Drums are heard, so use an ear word', 'Your hands can find out, even with no looking'.

readability.evidence: Kid text reads at FK grade -1.2 (family limit 5.0) in two- to five-word sentences of everyday words (eyes, ears, soft, loud, taste). Adult text is FK 9.5 (limit 10.0). Lab lines are one short sentence with a big emoji picture for every thing and body part, so a pre-reader can play with an adult reading aloud; body-part tiles carry both a picture and the word.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs each teach one move: the five helpers, finding out with eyes shut, saying a sense word, and the tasting rule. Adult paragraphs give the goal and body parts, what each lab step does, the named common mistakes plus the skin nuance, and the safety rule with examples. The sorter practises sorting words by sense, which no lab step repeats.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 dark and 360 px Android light screenshots of every step plus mid-task shots of the bag, the sort boxes and the pine cone. Five body-part tiles fit in one row at 360 px with emoji and label readable (about 64 px wide and 70 px tall); food and look-only boxes hold sorted items without overlap; the phone sweep reported 0 findings. Fixed the lowest pine-cone scale line spilling below the cone.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin (send to each body part, Feel, each toy, each sense word, Food to taste and Look only, explore with each part), so dragging is never required. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action, e.g. 'Which part helps with a bell? Parts: eyes, ears, nose, mouth, hands' and 'It feels hard and cold. Is it the teddy, rock or sponge?'. Challenge feedback sits in a polite live region with a text tick or cross; axe WCAG 2.1 AA was clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
